title: Transactions: correctness under concurrency
lead: North has 40 boxes and South has 60. Moving five boxes needs two writes. We will follow what another reader can see between those writes, then build a test for whether an interleaving is safe.
goals: Construct a precedence graph from a read/write schedule
Distinguish conflict serializability from view serializability

sections.title: Why two writes must form one piece of work
sections.html:
Our running example is an original warehouse transfer. North contains 40 boxes and South 60; the total is 100. Transfer five boxes by first writing North=35, then South=65. After both writes, the total is still 100. Stop after the first, however, and the database says only 95 boxes exist.

We therefore draw a boundary around the two writes: BEGIN; subtract at North; add at South; COMMIT. This bounded unit is a transaction. COMMIT accepts its changes; ABORT, also called ROLLBACK, removes its database effects. The application may request an abort, or the DBMS may require one.

Four separate promises are useful here. Atomicity prevents a half-transfer surviving an abort. Consistency means preserving the application's rules, such as total=100; the programmer must still write the correct addition. Isolation, under the serializability model used in this lesson, makes concurrent work behave like some order of complete transactions. Durability keeps an acknowledged commit after the failures covered by the system's assumptions.

A simple starting design runs one transaction at a time and changes a private copy. It is easy to reason about but delays unrelated work and copies too much data. Interleaving lets the CPU serve one transaction while another waits for storage. That benefit creates the observation problem in the next section.

Two implementation questions remain separate: locking or optimistic validation controls interference; logging or shadow copies support undo and durable completion. A conflict-graph proof will not prove crash durability. Database rollback also cannot recall a truck that has already left: external effects need an application protocol.

Logging records enough history to reverse an aborted change or reconstruct a committed one. Shadow paging instead edits copies and publishes the replacement pages at commit. For isolation, pessimistic control prevents harmful access in advance; optimistic control lets work proceed separately, then validates and may abort when conflicts are found. The latter is attractive when conflicts are uncommon, not a promise that conflicts cannot happen.

The application subtracts five at North but accidentally adds four at South. Can ACID infer the missing box?

Worked answer. No. Atomicity can commit or remove that whole transaction, but cannot invent the intended business calculation. Consistency requires correct transaction logic and applicable integrity checks.

sections.title: Watch a reader between the writes
sections.html:
T1 transfers five boxes; T2 reports the total. If T2 runs entirely before T1, it reads 40+60=100. If it runs entirely afterward, it reads 35+65=100. These are the two serial orders: transactions run one after another.

Now preserve the order inside each transaction, but interleave their operations. A schedule records this execution order; local arithmetic is omitted from its read/write notation.

StepDatabase (North,South)What happens
0(40,60)Initial state
1(35,60)T1 writes North=35
2(35,60)T2 reads North: 35
3(35,60)T2 reads South: 60; reports 95
4(35,65)T1 writes South=65 and commits

The final database has 100 boxes, yet T2 has already returned 95. Its two individually valid reads combined two different stages of the transfer. This is why comparing only final contents is too weak.

We want an interleaved schedule to be equivalent to some serial order: this is serializability. The equivalent order need not be transaction start order or commit order. It must preserve the relevant observations and effects. Later sections make “equivalent” precise in two ways.

Concurrency is useful for independent work. A transaction reading an unrelated product can run during this transfer without creating this anomaly. The challenge is to order accesses that can actually affect one another, rather than serialize the entire database.

Move T1’s South write before T2’s South read, leaving T2’s North read after the subtraction. What total does T2 report?

Worked answer. It reads 35+65=100. This fixes this observation, but a general correctness test must inspect every conflicting pair, rather than accept a schedule because one chosen arithmetic result happens to match.

sections.title: Turn conflicting operations into ordering constraints
sections.html:
Write R1(X) for “T1 reads X” and W2(Y) for “T2 writes Y.” Two reads of X do not change each other's values. Operations on different objects are also independent in this model. But a write and another transaction's read/write of the same object cannot in general change places without changing an observation or the final writer. That pair conflicts.

Consider R1(X), W1(X), R2(X), W2(Y), R1(Y). Put one node per transaction in a graph. Examine earlier/later pairs from different transactions on the same object:

ObjectConflicting pairRequired serial order
XW1(X) before R2(X)T1 → T2
YW2(Y) before R1(Y)T2 → T1

The arrow means “must be before,” not “currently waiting.” The two arrows demand both T1 before T2 and T2 before T1. No serial order can satisfy that cycle. This precedence graph, also called a conflict graph, characterizes conflict serializability: an acyclic graph permits a serial order; a cycle rules it out.

Change the ending to R1(Y), W2(Y). Now every edge points T1→T2, so T1,T2 is valid. The graph summarizes repeated constraints; adding the same edge twice changes nothing. Adjacent operations from different transactions can be swapped when they do not conflict, while preserving each transaction's own order. For example, R2(B) and W1(A) can swap when A≠B.

For three transactions, R2(A), W2(A), R1(A), R1(B), W1(B), R3(B), W3(B) gives T2→T1 on A and T1→T3 on B. Following the arrows yields T2,T1,T3. Such an ordering is a topological order.

Key takeaway

A cycle rules out conflict serializability. Each edge imposes an order between two transactions, and a cycle makes those ordering requirements contradictory.

For R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B), and independent R3(C), list every possible serial order.

Worked answer. Both conflicts impose T1→T2. T3 touches only C, so it has no edge: (T3,T1,T2), (T1,T3,T2), and (T1,T2,T3) are all valid. Starting earlier does not determine T3’s serial position.

sections.title: Read values, commit order, and three kinds of failure
sections.html:
A conflict is an ordering relationship; an anomaly is an unwanted behavior it can permit. Follow the values, not just the labels:

CaseTraceWhy it is a problem
Unrepeatable readT1 reads price=100; T2 writes 80 and commits; T1 reads 80One transaction gets different values on repeated reads
Dirty readT1 writes 80 without committing; T2 reads 80T2 depends on a result that can still be removed
Lost updateSeats=8; T1 reads 8; T2 reads 8; T1 writes 7; T2 writes 7Two bookings should leave 6, but the second write loses a decrement

The seat schedule is R1(S), R2(S), W1(S), W2(S). R1 before W2 gives T1→T2; R2 before W1 gives T2→T1; W1 before W2 repeats T1→T2. Its graph has a cycle. A dirty read is dirty at the time of reading even if the writer later commits.

What if a transaction aborts?

The following supplementary bridge separates recovery dependencies from serializability. Let C1 mean T1 commits, A1 mean T1 aborts. These are events, not objects named C or A.

  1. W1(A), R2(A), C2, A1: T2 has committed using a value that must disappear. This is not recoverable.
  2. W1(A), R2(A), C1, C2: the dirty read remains, but the dependent reader waits to commit until its writer commits. This is recoverable.
  3. W1(A), C1, R2(A), C2: the reader waits even to read. This is cascadeless: it avoids reading values that may need undo.

A strict schedule also prevents overwriting another transaction's uncommitted write. Strict implies cascadeless, which implies recoverable. In W1(A), W2(A), C2, C1 there are no reads, so the cascadeless read condition holds, but W2 is a dirty write: the schedule is not strict. Commit dependencies and graph acyclicity answer different questions.

Key takeaway

A dirty read is identified at the moment of the read. If T1 later commits, the earlier read is still dirty. If T1 aborts, the price returns to 100, but T2 may already have used 80 in its calculation.

Can a recoverable schedule still require cascading aborts before its writer commits?

Worked answer. Yes. In W1(A), R2(A), C1, C2 the commit order is recoverable, but R2 is dirty. If T1 aborts instead of reaching C1, T2 must discard work derived from that value. Waiting only at commit does not prevent the dirty dependency.

sections.title: When a conflict cycle is too strong a rejection
sections.html:
The graph test is convenient because it ignores actual values and checks all conflicting pairs. Can it reject an interleaving whose observations still match a serial execution? Consider an original example with no reads: W1(X), W2(X), W1(X). The first two writes create T1→T2 and the last two create T2→T1. The graph has a cycle.

But nobody reads either intermediate value. T1 writes X last. Serial order T2,T1 also has no reads and T1 as final writer. The schedules are view-equivalent: preserve each initial-value read, each read's source transaction, and each object's final writer. A write performed without first reading that object is a blind write; these writes explain the gap between the criteria.

Now add a read: R1(A), W2(A), W1(A), W3(A). Track the two required observations:

View conditionOriginal scheduleSerial order T1,T2,T3
Source of R1(A)Initial valueInitial value
Final writer of AT3T3

It remains view-serializable despite a T1↔T2 conflict cycle. T1 reads A before its own write; T2 and T3 make blind writes. Intermediate writes have no dependent reads.

Do not infer that every cycle is harmless. In R1(A), W2(A), R1(A), T1 first reads the initial value, then T2's value. Put all of T1 before T2 and the second source is lost; put it after T2 and the initial read is lost. Neither serial order works.

Conflict serializability is thus sufficient for view serializability, while the converse fails. The efficient graph criterion supports practical scheduling, but it proves that particular criterion. It does not replace checking abort handling, durability, or the application's own logic.

Key takeaway

An acyclic graph characterizes conflict serializability. A cycle alone does not disprove view serializability: the blind-write example here still preserves every read source and final writer.

Does a cyclic precedence graph prove that no view-equivalent serial execution exists?

Worked answer. No. W1(X), W2(X), W1(X) is the counterexample: the view conditions match T2,T1. To reject view serializability, inspect read sources and final writers rather than reusing the cycle test.

quiz.question: Is R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B) conflict-serializable?
options: Yes, in the order T1 then T2
Yes, in the order T2 then T1
No, because the graph has a cycle
There is insufficient information because two objects are involved
quiz.explanation: Both R1(A) before W2(A) and W1(B) before R2(B) create T1 → T2. There is no edge in the reverse direction.

source.summary: Lecture 19 introduces transactions, ACID, execution schedules, conflicts, and two serializability criteria. A dependency graph checks conflict serializability, while logging or shadow paging supports atomicity and durability.
